title: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Text Sequences
summary: This document describes the JSON text sequence format and the media type application/json-seq. A sequence is any number of JSON texts, encoded in UTF-8, each prefixed by an ASCII Record Separator character. This helps stream many JSON values one after another.

eli5.summary: Imagine a long ribbon of messages with a special mark before each one. This lets a program read them as they arrive instead of waiting for the end.

questions: how to stream multiple json texts
what is a json text sequence
why does json-seq use the record separator character
how to parse truncated json in a sequence
subtitle: A way to stream many JSON values one after another, with a marker byte that lets readers recover from damage.

tldr.problem: Plain JSON is awkward for huge, open-ended or never-ending series of values, because a reader normally needs a streaming parser or has to read everything before producing results.
tldr.mechanism: A JSON text sequence is any number of UTF-8 JSON texts, each preceded by an ASCII Record Separator (0x1E) and followed by a Line Feed (0x0A), so a reader can split the stream at each separator and parse one piece at a time.
tldr.outcome: Readers can process elements incrementally and skip damaged ones, and the format has its own media type, application/json-seq. It is a Proposed Standard with no replacement or update listed.

today: RFC 7464 is a Proposed Standard, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It is therefore still the definition of the JSON text sequence format and the application/json-seq media type.

sections.title: Why JSON Needs Sequences
sections.content:
RFC 7159 defines JSON, a handy serialization format. But when you need to send a large series of values as one array, or a series of indeterminate length or one that never ends, JSON gets hard to work with. The RFC gives an example of one million values of roughly one kilobyte each, around one gigabyte in total, which you would like to process without reading it all first.

The usual answer is a streaming parser, but the RFC notes these are not widely available, widely used or easy to use. A JSON text sequence is the alternative. It is specifically not a JSON text itself. It is a series of pieces that are each possibly a JSON text, and it can be parsed and produced incrementally without a streaming parser or a streaming encoder.
sections.eli5: Reading a giant list all at once is like trying to swallow a whole pizza. This format cuts the pizza into slices so you can eat one slice at a time.

sections.title: How to Write a Sequence
sections.content:
An encoder writes any number of JSON texts. Each one is encoded in UTF-8, preceded by one ASCII Record Separator (RS, byte 0x1E) and followed by a Line Feed (LF, byte 0x0A). The ABNF is JSON-sequence = *(RS JSON-text LF). Other encodings of JSON, UTF-16 and UTF-32, MUST NOT be used.

The separator works because RS is an ASCII control character. Inside a JSON string it can only appear in escaped form, and it cannot appear in a JSON text in any other form, so RS unambiguously marks the start of every element. RS alone is enough to delimit every top-level JSON value type except numbers, and the trailing LF covers that gap (see the section on top-level values).

Encoders are expected to make sure each element is well formed. If the encoder is handed already-encoded JSON texts, it ought to parse them before adding them to the sequence. To build a sequence by hand in a text editor, some systems let you type RS as ctrl-^, and others need ctrl-v ctrl-^.
sections.eli5: Each message gets a special stamp in front and a line break at the end. The stamp is a character that can never show up inside a message, so you always know where a new message starts.

sections.title: How to Read a Sequence
sections.content:
The parser rules are looser than the encoder rules on purpose. The parser grammar is input-JSON-sequence = *(1*RS possible-JSON): a series of octet strings, each containing any octet other than RS, and each preceded by RS. Every octet string is then interpreted as a UTF-8 JSON text, if possible.

Several RS bytes in a row do not mean empty elements between them, and can be ignored. There is no end-of-sequence indicator. The RFC also warns that it defines no way to identify an element by position, so a reference to the nth element would be unreliable where truncation is possible, because elements can be truncated or even missing entirely.
sections.eli5: The reader looks for the stamps, then reads whatever is between two stamps as one message. Extra stamps in a row are just ignored.

sections.title: Surviving Broken Elements
sections.content:
If an octet string fails to parse as a UTF-8 JSON text, the parser SHOULD still continue with the rest of the sequence. It may report the failure to the application, which can choose to stop. In practice the parser skips ahead to the next RS.

The RFC's example of when this happens is log data appended to a file and then cut short by the filesystem, for instance after a crash or an administrator terminating a process. Incremental JSON parsers may be used, though a failure may come only after some partial results were already produced. Sequence parsers should also have an option to warn about truncated JSON texts.
sections.eli5: If one message on the ribbon is torn, you do not throw the whole ribbon away. You skip to the next stamp and keep going.

sections.title: Numbers, true, false and null
sections.content:
Objects, arrays and strings mark their own ends, but numbers and the values true, false and null do not. Only whitespace can end them. That matters because a cut-off 1234 looks like a complete 123. The RFC uses the LF byte as a canary to detect this kind of truncation.

Parsers MUST check that any top-level number, or anything that might be true, false or null, is followed by at least one JSON whitespace byte. Parsers MUST drop elements of this kind that are not delimited by whitespace, and can report them as warnings. The RFC's examples: <RS>123<RS> might have been meant to carry 1234, <RS>true<RS> might have been meant to carry the invalid text trueish, and <RS>truefalse<RS> is not two values but simply not valid JSON.

This check only works when the sequence encoder produces or receives complete JSON texts. If it does not encode the individual texts itself, it should ensure they are complete.
sections.eli5: If a message just says 12 and the rest got cut off, it might have been 1234. The line break at the end is a sign that the message really finished.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All the security considerations of JSON apply, and the format provides no cryptographic integrity protection of any kind. Parsers must treat input as untrusted and fail gracefully on malicious input.

Two specific risks are named. First, an incremental parser may return a partial result and only later fail, so a sequence like <RS>"foo"<LF>456<LF><RS> could be seen as one element by an incremental parser and as empty by a non-incremental one. That difference, and texts that fail to parse and are ignored, can be used to smuggle data past parsers that do not warn about failures. Second, repeatedly parsing and re-encoding a sequence can add or strip trailing LF bytes, which can break signature validation. JSON has no canonical form, so neither does this format.
sections.eli5: A sneaky sender could hide something in a smudged message that one reader skips and another reads. And this format has no lock, so anyone could change the ribbon without it showing.

sections.title: The Media Type
sections.content:
The RFC registers the media type application/json-seq. It has no required or optional parameters, its encoding consideration is binary, and its intended usage is listed as COMMON. The change controller is the IETF.

The registration also lists a few applications that use the type, naming the jq tool and two other projects by their addresses.
sections.eli5: The format gets an official name tag, application/json-seq, so programs can tell each other what kind of data is coming.

data.title: JSON text sequence encoder grammar
data.code:
JSON-sequence = *(RS JSON-text LF)
RS = %x1E; "record separator" (RS), see RFC 20
LF = %x0A; "line feed" (LF), see RFC 20
JSON-text = <given by RFC 7159, using UTF-8 encoding>

viz.caption: THE TRUNCATION RULES AT A GLANCE

items.title: Self-delimited
items.text: Objects, arrays and strings mark their own end.

items.title: Not self-delimited
items.text: Numbers, true, false and null need whitespace after them.

items.title: LF canary
items.text: The LF after each text counts as that whitespace.

items.title: Parser duty
items.text: Parsers MUST drop such elements if no whitespace follows.
